items.question: How did your experience of AI conference peer review lead you to leave AI algorithm research?
items.object: AI conference peer review and the pursuit of academic publication
items.answer:
The first is that I think academia is now in a state of collapsing rites and music—of serious disorder. When I first entered AI research, around 2018, an academic conference might receive only several hundred papers a year. I thought the scholarly community was healthier then: after submitting a paper, reviewers could give relatively constructive, positive feedback, telling you what was good, what was not, and how to improve. We were genuinely discussing how to make work better. Later, however, conference scale expanded far faster than the community grew. AI conference submissions rose geometrically every year. Obviously, both the number and quality of reviewers fell far behind the number of submissions. Review quality then dropped sharply, and submitting a paper became like buying a lottery ticket: whether it was accepted might no longer have much to do with the quality of the work itself.

I witnessed that process firsthand, so it is painful to see. But I could not change a building that was about to collapse by myself. So I left AI algorithm research and stopped treating publication as my pursuit.

items.object: Kaiming He’s success in AI algorithm research
items.answer: Besides his exceptional ability, my conclusion was that what he did was not only simple and effective in method; he also conducted large-scale experiments. We little fish in the lab were just playing with toy datasets—making a spectacle inside a snail shell, doing tricks on a tiny dataset—without large-scale experimentation. items.question: How did your conversation with Professor Zhang Qiangyu change your understanding of the engineering challenges in machine-learning systems?
items.object: The engineering challenges of machine-learning systems revealed by his conversation with Professor Zhang Qiangyu
items.answer: He was patient enough to talk with me for more than an hour. At the time he was at Megvii, probably its chief scientist. I was surprised to find that, as a leading figure in object-detection algorithms, he was not talking about a new object-detection loss or its effects. He talked more about the challenges complex hardware created for software, and how Megvii had to design hardware specialized for object-detection and CV algorithms. Such hardware had multilevel cache structures, and you had to manually control data movement between the chip’s multiple cache levels. So what troubled Megvii engineers most every day was not how to tune parameters, but that NVIDIA cuDNN code had this problem or that problem, and they needed to write this operator or that operator to suit the hardware. That had a major impact on me. It helped push me from algorithm research toward engineering research on machine-learning systems.

items.answer:
I began my PhD in 2020, when large models were already developing—2020 should have been when GPT-3 was released. But our lab’s compute resources were very limited, so we could not conduct large-scale pretraining experiments. Based on the compute we could command, I researched methods such as large-model fine-tuning. After doing that for a while, there were some results, but it had a similar problem to before: it was more icing on the cake.

We might spend a year researching various algorithms and improve results by one or two percentage points in the original setting. But a year later, someone has a better, larger pretrained model; simply replacing the pretrained model produces a bigger gain than my algorithm. So, together with the reasons I mentioned, in the latter half of my PhD I switched from AI algorithm research to AI machine-learning systems research.

items.question: How do you understand the role of fortunate coincidences in the path that brought you to machine-learning systems and vLLM?

I told him that I had actually asked him this question four years earlier, and that in those four years I had kept exploring what I could do, and whether anyone would use interesting things I built. I think I would still have moved from algorithm research to machine-learning systems. I had been cultivating this major decision for several years.

items.question: How do you understand Berkeley’s tradition of producing open-source projects that become industrial infrastructure?

items.answer: I think the lab inherits a certain historical lineage. Including my work on vLLM, I think it is influenced by Berkeley’s tradition of heavy-duty industrial software. Berkeley has a long history of open-source software, including BSD in operating systems, RISC-V in chips, RAID in storage, and later Spark and Ray in big data and distributed machine-learning systems. They all came from Berkeley. These programs were initiated while students were enrolled: they began as student research projects, then were primarily maintained by students, grew their communities, and became infrastructure in industry. On this point, we can mention a leading computer-architecture researcher, David Patterson. In 2014, he wrote an opinion paper called “How to Build a Bad Research Center.” Based on his decades of experience, he said that each lab or large research center only needs to last five years, because that is exactly one PhD graduation cycle. If you fully use excellent PhD students during those five years, allowing them to calmly focus on one field, it can greatly advance that field. So AMPLab made Spark, then RISE Lab made Ray, and later came Sky Lab. Berkeley’s labs thus develop in one continuous lineage. When their five-year cycles resonate with cycles of industry demand, important projects are born, such as Spark.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between material comfort and spiritual fulfillment in vLLM’s early team?

items.question: How do you characterize vLLM’s development across 2024 and 2025?
items.object: vLLM’s development in 2024 and 2025
items.answer: I think the main theme of 2024 was really a reconstruction. Because the paper was published in 2023, and then a prototype came out in 2023. Then this prototype needed to go from an experimental prototype to something production-grade and usable. In that process, we studied the designs of many other inference engines in the industry, and ultimately, at the end of the year, launched a reconstruction plan from V0 to V1. Then the main theme of 2025 was deployment at scale: hardware and models both became bigger and bigger, and the center of gravity for open-source-model development shifted from Europe and the United States to China. I happened to return from Berkeley, so I built the Chinese vLLM community from scratch. And that also happened to support the release of a large number of Chinese open-source models.

items.question: How do you understand the engineering significance of vLLM’s V0-to-V1 reconstruction when the user experience changed so little?
items.object: The engineering significance of vLLM’s V0-to-V1 reconstruction
items.answer:
This reconstruction was mainly intended to address new challenges that the development of models and hardware posed for inference engines. For an analogy, people now often like to compare tokens to electricity. In that process, the inference engine is like a generator. Or rather, an electric-power system. Actually, I think the model may be more like the generator; we can make some analogies later. And hardware is like natural resources such as wind and solar power. What the inference system needs to do is use a generator to turn those natural resources into electricity, and then deliver it into everyone's hands. So this reconstruction was like transitioning the overall power-generation system from coal-fired power to new-energy generation. From the user's perspective, the way of using it may not differ much: it is still electricity, right? You plug it in and use it. But from the inference engine's perspective, the underlying operating principles changed enormously.

So from an end user's perspective, the inference engine takes on a major responsibility: it hides the complexity of models and hardware. When users select different models—for example, an application may support multiple models—from the user's perspective they may simply select a model from a dropdown menu, or change one request parameter and say, hey, today I'm requesting DeepSeek, tomorrow Qwen. But from the perspective of the inference engine behind it, different models vary enormously in support efficiency and in the hardware they are suited to. So the inference engine takes on an extremely important task here. And models and hardware keep evolving in this process, so their requirements for inference engines are constantly changing. V0 and V1 are simply a very large change, as you can tell from the names, but we have actually been making similar smaller changes all along. So you could say vLLM has always been in the process of reconstruction. The hardest part is maintaining user compatibility. Right? The models and hardware supported behind the scenes keep changing, but you have to give front-end end users a relatively unified experience: with vLLM, I can be assured that I can run all kinds of models on all kinds of hardware.

items.question: Why did you see a need for a Chinese-language vLLM community when the existing Slack community was open to everyone?
items.object: Building the Chinese-language vLLM community
items.answer:
This project itself was born in the United States. And the main open-source base in 2024 was also in the United States. So the overall communication channels were U.S.-leaning; for example, we used Slack to communicate. Later, when we communicated with people in China, we said to everyone that the vLLM community is a very inclusive community, and students in China and the U.S. can all communicate together. We have Slack as a communication mechanism, and everyone can join. But there were two problems. First, people in China are certainly more accustomed to speaking Chinese, while people mainly speak English in Slack, which creates a language barrier. Second, for various reasons, there are still inconveniences for people in China using overseas software. So to solve these problems, we began building Chinese-language vLLM communities, including outreach platforms such as WeChat official accounts, Xiaohongshu, and Zhihu, as well as channels for communication and contact with some large Chinese companies.

Companies like DeepSeek and Kimi have publicly said that they use vLLM. Previously, we had very little communication with them, because of the time-zone difference and because there was no way for people to meet. After I returned to China, I visited these companies and learned what they were doing with vLLM, what problems they encountered, and what pain points they had. Because I had done a lot of work on vLLM in 2024 and everyone knew me fairly well, I connected everyone this way.

items.question: How do you see the role of donating vLLM to the PyTorch Foundation in sustaining the project over the long term?
items.object: Donating vLLM to the PyTorch Foundation
items.answer:
We were discussing this at the end of 2024. The background was really the project's long-term maintenance; we were considering how it would be maintained over the long term. Then Professor Jan Stoica said that we should have a company supporting the project, otherwise the project would eventually die. But several of us were still hesitant, and whether the project could find a long-term maintainer was itself a question. So Professor Jan Stoica said that we should follow the experience of projects like Linux and donate it to a foundation. That way, its long-term open-source status and maintenance could be ensured. So it was donated to the PyTorch Foundation, because we also worked closely with PyTorch.

PyTorch is, in effect, an underlying machine-learning framework, and vLLM is an inference engine built on top of it, so that collaboration was natural. But the PyTorch Foundation itself is more of a governance-oriented foundation; it does not participate in your technical governance, so you still have to write the code yourself. It is more that donating the project to the foundation means that it will at least not become closed source; it will remain open source.

items.question: Why did you believe vLLM's long-term development required a company to support it?

items.answer: For the few of us, forming the company was actually quite difficult. Because Professor Jan Stoica had a very firm belief: for such a large project, if there is no company supporting it, it will certainly die. He said that without Red Hat's support, Linux would not have developed into what it is today. Likewise, without Google's support, Kubernetes would not have developed into what it is today. Likewise, without Meta's support, PyTorch would not have developed into what it is today. You could cite many, many more examples. Spark has Databricks' support. And vLLM had already reached the scale of the projects I mentioned; its historical significance was already clear, yet there was no such company supporting it. Other companies in the community might not accept Meta's leadership. So it would be difficult to do this under their leadership. Therefore, it was very clear that the long-term development of vLLM required a company's support. We all agreed with that. What we needed to determine was whether we were willing to found that company. That was actually a difficult decision. I can talk about each of our thought processes. items.question: How do you think about your decision to remove beam search from the inference engine despite users’ objections?
items.object: Removing beam search from the inference engine as a benevolent dictator
items.answer: Being a benevolent dictator means that sometimes you need to make tradeoffs about direction. You cannot be a people pleaser. One relatively hard-line choice I made was to essentially remove a feature called beam search from the engine. People continually come and complain about this, especially people working on recommendation systems. Their experience is that beam search is important in their scenarios. But what we see is that for large-model inference—the main workflow on the AI side—the form of inference no longer fits the development of algorithms like beam search. So if we continued maintaining beam-search algorithms, it would only bring more and more complexity to adaptation between models and the inference engine, making it unmaintainable. So I removed it.

items.question: How do you think the rise of coding agents is changing what it takes to manage a large open-source community like vLLM?
items.object: Managing large open-source communities as coding agents make code contributions easier
items.answer:
I think the biggest challenge is sorting out priorities. What to do, and more importantly what not to do. When a project has more than 2,000 contributors—especially this year, when coding agents have become very popular—contributing code has become extremely easy. So as project managers, the most important thing we need to do is filter out noise, find the things truly worth doing, and guide the community in that direction.

There is one data point: in 2025, GitHub published statistics that ranked projects by contributor activity, and vLLM was the most active project on all of GitHub. On the one hand, we are honored; on the other, this brings what we call happy troubles. For example, in May this year, we found that some training institutions were padding their students' résumés by submitting junk code: they would submit an unhelpful PR and want it merged into vLLM. Then they could say on a student's résumé that the student was a vLLM project contributor, hoping to improve the odds that the résumé would pass interviews. This was a major change for us: it completely shattered our fundamental assumption that users of open-source communities are all acting in good faith. So now we can only introduce some verification mechanisms. For example, we place more importance on contributions from well-known institutions, and we ignore or even block accounts that look very much like bots—for example, one that submits 20 PRs in ten minutes. Such a person must be a bot, and there is no human involvement in what they submit; it is all coding agents, what we call AI slop. It is entirely devoid of substance, so you can safely block it.

I think that as AI and coding agents develop, the future direction of open-source communities will be increasingly controlled by institutions and important contributors. Individual contributors will actually be able to do less. Overall, code has become so cheap that, for a maintainer, rather than spending time reviewing someone else's PR, it is better to have a coding agent write it again themselves. And maintainers themselves have more context about how they want the coding agent to write it. So I think future open-source communities will place more emphasis on feedback. A community will become two parts: maintainers and users. Users only need to submit bug reports or feature requests; they only need to say what problem they encountered while using it, or what else they want to use. They do not need to contribute code; maintainers can contribute the code themselves.

items.question: Why do you think vLLM maintenance cannot yet be fully automated with AI?
items.object: Fully automating vLLM maintenance with AI
items.answer: In our case, it is still difficult to fully automate with AI. We still need many participants' historical insight. Many things we do are not to solve an existing problem; often, they solve problems that are about to occur. For example, we need to support new models that will be released within the next three months. So when maintaining code, we do not just look at how it supports existing models; we must also be thinking about how the models we will support in the next three months will be supported in this code. And that includes how to support new hardware coming out in the next half year or the next year. So maintaining this project must be done with a great deal of personal context. That part cannot yet be handed over to AI.

items.question: How do you see the difficulty of sustaining open-source infrastructure projects without a company behind them?
items.object: Support and maintenance of open-source infrastructure
items.answer: I think there are quite a lot of such examples, especially open-source communities that do not have a company supporting them behind the scenes. For example, many famous projects in history have actually been struggling to survive on the efforts of just a few people. OpenSSH, for example, is computer infrastructure everyone needs; it provides SSH encryption and decryption, yet it had only a few maintainers maintaining it themselves. Then, roughly more than ten years ago, an incident occurred: one of its vulnerabilities was cracked, potentially leaving the whole world exposed—everyone might be able to see your password. Only after that happened did people establish a foundation and put some money into supporting its maintenance. Open-source community infrastructure has always been an old, recurring topic: these projects are all important, but until they have problems, everyone thinks there is no need to invest.

items.question: Why did you come to believe that vLLM could no longer continue without a company's support around 2025?
items.object: The need for company support to sustain vLLM around 2025
items.answer:
Around 2025, our main task was deploying large models at scale, at the cluster level. At that point, we encountered many problems. On the one hand, there was the human-resources issue. When operating as an open-source community, the people participating in these things are uncertain: people come and go, right? Some arrive, some newly join, and others leave. That cannot support sustained work on an important feature over the long term.

On the other hand, there were legal issues: our work with many companies involved confidentiality. Because we often support new model releases before they happen, as well as new hardware releases before they happen. In that process, the other side's legal team often requires an NDA, a non-disclosure agreement, right? Who signs that NDA was an awkward question, because an open-source community is not an entity. So the other side's legal team would often ask who was behind the work. They might also need to check: these people are working on it this time, but a different group may work on it next time. Among the people who changed, are there any competitors of ours? Do we need to conduct background checks before allowing them access to this information? These are all things an open-source project cannot do.

In addition to human resources, there was also the issue of machine resources. For large-scale deployment of large models, why was this less prominent in 2024? Because models were smaller then; if you could get one machine, a single machine with a single card could do a lot. Some companies were also enthusiastic and generous enough to donate us some machines. But by 2025, because the overall scale had increased, many optimizations we needed to do had to be at the cluster level. It was very difficult to ask someone to give me a cluster; giving me one machine was already the utmost support they could offer. So to do cluster-level optimization, we could only go around begging. I might first need to spend a month persuading the other side to give me the machines. After getting them, I had to plan nonstop: I would do these things today and those things tomorrow, because the machines might expire after one month. And their giving us the machines was not a promised arrangement. If they had an urgent project internally, perhaps in a week they would use them themselves on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and let you use them on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. They might even urgently notify you that they would need them within the next hour. So these things created major obstacles.

To be honest, I do not think we had much fun doing things in 2025. These circumstances made it very clear to us that without a company's support, the project could no longer continue.

items.question: How do you think about raising capital for the company you formed around vLLM?
items.object: Fundraising for the company formed around vLLM
items.answer:
I think that part went relatively smoothly. Silicon Valley VCs had overall been waiting for us for a long time. Although we decided to form the company at the end of 2025, they had actually been in contact with us in 2023 and 2024, and had already been providing funds to our open-source project then. One thing worth emphasizing here is that ACC, for example, provided a grant to the vLLM project in 2023. It was a pure grant to support the development of the open-source project. At the time, it should have been on the order of several hundred thousand U.S. dollars. Then in 2024, Sequoia and ZhenFund both donated money to us in the form of an open-source community. So they noticed us very early, and they recognized, like we did, that vLLM was an important project. They were willing to invest some early resources to support us. Of course, they also said that if we started a company, they would definitely support us strongly. So when we finally announced that the few of us had decided to start a company and went back to them, they were all quite ready and said, actually, I have already prepared the money. They had been waiting for us all along, actually.

So although the amount we raised in the seed round was relatively large, overall it was still a stage where investors were proactively coming to us to invest. Even after we finished the seed round, people have continued to say even now: I have a lot of money here; I can give it to you directly—SAFE financing in the tens of millions of dollars. And consider us in your next round of financing. But we are still cautiously optimistic. We hope to match financing with the speed of the company's growth. We are not fundraising for the sake of fundraising. It is not that we have to take money just because money is available now. It is more about looking at what stage the company has reached and what we need to use the money for. Then we consider the next round.

items.question: How do you think forming a company changes your ability to organize work compared with running an open-source community?
items.object: The transition from running an open-source community to running a company
items.answer: I think a company really is quite different. When we were running the open-source community before, one difficult thing was that you could not force certain things forward from the top down; you could not really make plans. Because the people participating may all have their own jobs, so they are not doing this full time. They may have other internal matters—for example, urgent things—and then they cannot come today. So we could only operate on a best-efforts basis, or a wishful basis: “Please, everyone, finish this this week,” right? Now that we have a company, these people are all our full-time employees, right, and we have dedicated resources to move these things forward. So we can introduce more planning. We can say what we will complete this quarter, assign it to this group, and say what this group should do in the coming week. We can do more planning.

items.question: How would you explain co-design between model architecture and inference infrastructure using the analogy of tokens as electricity?
items.object: Co-design between model architecture and inference infrastructure
items.answer: I think we can perhaps start from that analogy. I think models can be compared to generators: there are wind-turbine generators, photovoltaic solar generators, and mechanical hydropower generators. And the inference engine can be compared to the power system: it runs the model on the hardware. Then it sends those tokens to users and distributes them to households. items.question: Why do you think model architecture and inference infrastructure need to be designed together?
items.object: Co-design between model architecture and inference infrastructure
items.answer: To explain this clearly, we probably need to clarify a concept called the hardware lottery. Several decades ago, when Moore's law was still relatively effective, software and hardware development were basically proceeding independently. If you wrote software, you did not need to consider so many hardware characteristics, because general-purpose hardware performance doubled every two years, and software performance naturally became faster along with it. But the problem now is that the golden age of Moore's law has ended: you can no longer get general-purpose performance improvements through process technology. So we have now entered a specialized era. NVIDIA often talks about Huang's law: your compute power may multiply several times every two years. But this compute is specialized compute; it cannot be general purpose. So if your algorithm does not make use of that specialized compute, you have not won the hardware lottery. You do not get to enjoy the benefits of this era. For example, I think Professor Hinton, who is very senior in machine learning, strongly promoted something called Capsule Networks. He felt it made a great deal of sense conceptually, but it was not GPU-friendly, so it did not gain broad adoption—or, rather, it has not gained broad adoption to this day. To gain broad adoption, it might need specialized hardware. So a model's structure determines the upper bound of inference efficiency. If that upper bound is too low, systems engineers are powerless to turn things around, right? If you have already made it this bad, further optimization can only get it to this level. So you have to consider the two together.

items.question: Why do you see RoPE, or rotary positional encoding, as a good example of model architecture improving infrastructure efficiency?
items.object: RoPE (rotary positional encoding) and its co-design with attention infrastructure
items.answer: One relatively well-known example, I think, is RoPE, called rotary positional encoding. After Transformer emerged, for positional encoding, I think you could find at least a hundred implementations. But many of them require modifying the core attention implementation: if your positional encoding changes, your attention kernel needs to be rewritten. For example, there is a technique called ALiBi. It is an absolute position bias, so it did not gain broad adoption. One important reason RoPE became popular was that as training lengths increased, people needed positional encoding. At the same time, FlashAttention solved the training-length problem, so FlashAttention became necessary for training. At that point, most users had no way—and no ability—to modify FlashAttention, so most positional encodings that required modifying the internal implementation of attention were eliminated. No one tried them. RoPE's advantage is that it is an absolute positional encoding—people want an absolute positional encoding—but it is also a relative positional encoding, implemented in the manner of absolute positional encoding. So it has very good properties. It can also be injected independently into the query and key; it is independent of attention. You can perform RoPE independently outside the attention kernel, so it is complementary to the attention kernel. It thus became an ideal partner. So if a model architecture is well designed, it can have co-design with infra—a resonance effect, where each improves the other. With a more efficient implementation, your overall training and inference efficiency both improve substantially.

items.question: How do you assess the technical contribution of DeepSeek's DeSpark speculative-decoding method?
items.object: DeepSeek's DeSpark speculative-decoding method
items.answer: DeSpark is a new method of speculative decoding. For autoregressive large models, inference is divided into two stages: prefill and decoding. Prefill processes the user's input, while the decoding stage processes the model's own output. Because it is autoregressive, during decoding the model can only generate tokens one at a time, which is relatively inefficient. Speculative decoding means that, based on the current input, I guess several of the next tokens to be generated in one go, and turn the decoding process into short segments of prefill. It can then process multiple tokens at once and improve throughput. Before DeSpark was proposed, the industry had already researched many speculative-decoding methods. For example, the common Eagle, and MTP speculative decoding, also proposed by DeepSeek. Their characteristic is that the speculative length is relatively short, generally maybe three to five tokens, but the acceptance rate is high. DeSpark's technical route belongs to the DeFlash family. We have actually been following this area continuously over the past few months, so DeSpark is not especially novel to us. The defining feature of the DeFlash route is that it speculates many tokens at once, for example sixteen tokens. WM and NVIDIA actually just released a technical blog recently introducing DeFlash support in WM, which can reach speeds of thousands of tokens per second for certain models. The drawback of DeFlash is that it speculates many tokens, but it also guesses many incorrectly. Thus, there is a problem of wasted compute in the model-verification process. DeSpark's improvement to DeFlash is to estimate which of the speculated tokens are accurate and which are inaccurate, and then not verify tokens that are very likely inaccurate. So, for example, if the model speculates sixteen tokens—you can simply tally the confidence of the model's final output and perhaps find that only the first eight tokens are correct. Then you only need to verify the first eight tokens. So DeSpark roughly continues this line of work, improving DeFlash. DeSpark was not really surprising to us, because we had already been doing DeFlash-related optimization for several months, and the issue of DeFlash's acceptance rate is also a consensus in the DeFlash research community. Before DeSpark was proposed, Tencent's Huiyuan team had already published work called Decart, and students at Shanghai Jiao Tong had proposed work called Domino. Both use similar ideas to solve this problem. So, as for how novel DeSpark is algorithmically, I do not think it is very novel. We have also had a lot of communication with the DeepSeek team and Tencent Huiyuan team. Soon everyone will see WM support these algorithms as well. But innovation is one thing, and whether you can solidly implement an innovative idea is another. I think DeSpark inherits DeepSeek's consistently very solid infra foundation and squeezes inference optimization to the limit. This is also something we are learning from them: how to achieve better inference optimization. And this is another aspect of algorithm–infra co-design. Whether there is a good implementation in an inference engine is key to whether a speculative-decoding algorithm can be used at scale. DeepSeek's inference-engine team is extremely strong, so it also gives the algorithm team more room to explore speculative decoding and more feedback.
